pages.text: Noida Workers’ Protest

IBIBIC
‘How does one survive?': Factory
protests expose strain in India's
industrial system

Noida Workers’ Protest
•On April 13, 2026, a protest by thousands of factory workers in Noida
 escalated into widespread violence, paralyzing parts of the city’s industrial
 zones.
•The workers, demanding higher wages and improved working conditions, were
 reported to earn between ₹10,000 and ₹15,000 per month, wages that have
 remained largely unchanged for years.
•The unrest, which also spread to domestic workers in high-rise societies,
 triggered a massive security response and has become a significant crisis for the
 Uttar Pradesh government as the state heads towards elections.

Noida Workers’ Protest
•The most direct trigger was the Haryana government's decision to raise its
 minimum monthly wage by 35%, from approximately ₹14,000 to ₹19,000,
 prompting Noida workers to question why they earned significantly less (around
 ₹11,000–₹13,000) for similar work.
•A long-standing wage gap became an urgent survival issue due to a sharp rise in
 LPG cylinder prices and essential food items, driven by the ongoing West
 Asian crisis.
•Additionally, WhatsApp forwards in late March suggested that minimum wages
 would rise sharply under newly implemented Labour Codes, raising worker
 expectations that were not met.

Noida Workers’ Protest
•Protesters highlighted systemic violations of the eight-hour workday norm, arguing
 that 12-hour shifts have become standard in many Noida industrial units, with many
 workers forced to work extended hours without corresponding overtime pay or weekly
 off.
•Another major grievance is the informalization of the workforce, as even in large
 registered factories, many workers lack written contracts or job security, with middlemen
 and contractors often pocketing portions of their wages.
•Workers also face difficulties in accessing Employee Provident Fund (EPF) and
 insurance benefits, along with the absence of formal trade union representation,
 which has left them without a collective voice.

Noida Workers’ Protest
•The primary demand of the protesters was a minimum wage of ₹20,000 to
 ₹26,000 per month for unskilled workers, which they believe would better match
 the rising cost of living.
•Workers also demanded direct company hiring to prevent contractors from
 skimming wages, along with the strict implementation of double pay for every
 hour worked beyond the standard eight-hour shift.
•Other demands include the immediate clearance of pending bonuses, a significant
 increase in House Rent Allowance to address skyrocketing rents, and the
 establishment of functional Internal Complaints Committees to address
 workplace harassment.

Noida Workers’ Protest
Minimum Wages Act, 1948 –
•It is a central law that fixes minimum wages for workers in ‘scheduled
 employments’ to prevent exploitation.
•It provides for wage fixation including a basic rate and Variable Dearness
 Allowance (VDA), adjusted periodically for inflation.
•It empowers the government to fix normal working hours and mandates overtime
 at double the ordinary wage rate.

Noida Workers’ Protest
•Section 3 empowers the appropriate government to fix minimum rates of
 wages for any scheduled employment, while Section 5 outlines the procedure
 for fixing and revising these wages.
•Section 13 empowers the government to fix the number of hours for a normal
 working day, provide for a weekly day of rest, and mandate payment for work
 on a rest day.
•Section 14 mandates that any worker employed for more than the normal
 working day shall be entitled to overtime wages at a rate not less than twice
 the ordinary rate of wages.

Noida Workers’ Protest
The Code on Wages, 2019 –
•It consolidates four laws: Minimum Wages Act (1948), Payment of Wages Act
 (1936), Payment of Bonus Act (1965), and Equal Remuneration Act (1976).
•The Code universalizes minimum wages for all employees, moving away
 from the restrictive ‘scheduled employments’ concept.
•It introduces a statutory National Floor Wage based on minimum living
 standards, which no state can go below.

Noida Workers’ Protest
•The Code mandates that minimum wages fixed by central or state governments
 must be higher than the national floor wage, and existing wages higher than
 the floor cannot be reduced.
•It prohibits gender discrimination in matters related to wages and recruitment for
 the same work or work of a similar nature, promoting equality in the workplace.
•For overtime work, the Code stipulates that employees will be entitled to overtime
 wages at a rate at least twice the normal rate of wages, continuing the
 principle from the 1948 Act.

Noida Workers’ Protest
•While the Code on Wages was passed by Parliament in 2019 and received
 Presidential assent, its implementation has been delayed as states need to frame
 their own rules.
•However, the central government has operationalized key provisions of
 the Code, including the setting of the national floor wage, which is currently
 unskilled: ₹783, semi-skilled: ₹868, skilled: ₹958.
•The protests have pushed the central government to hasten the process of
 deciding a legally binding national floor wage, as the current non-statutory
 benchmark has been criticized for being too low.

Noida Workers’ Protest
Uttar Pradesh Minimum Wages Rules, 1952 –
•The Rules were framed under the powers granted by the Minimum Wages Act,
 1948, to regulate the payment of minimum wages in scheduled employments
 across the state.
•The Rules provide detailed procedures regarding wage fixation, payment,
 deductions, working hours, rest periods, and record maintenance to facilitate
 implementation and compliance.
•Despite the new Code on Wages, minimum wages in Uttar Pradesh are still
 primarily regulated by the 1952 Rules, as the state government has not yet
 fully transitioned to the new framework.

Noida Workers’ Protest
•Minimum wages in Uttar Pradesh are determined through a structured legal
 framework involving a fixed base wage with dynamic allowances, governed
 by the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, and the UP Minimum Wages Rules, 1952.


•The core wage structure is calculated based on norms established by the 15th
 Indian labour Conference (ILC), which ensures a worker can support a family
 of three consumption units (self, spouse, and two children).


•The state typically revises wages twice a year based on the Variable Dearness
 Allowance (VDA) , but workers argued that these routine adjustments were
 insufficient and left them with lower pay than in Delhi and Haryana.

Noida Workers’ Protest
•In direct response to the unrest, the Uttar Pradesh government announced
 an interim wage increase of 20-21% specifically for workers in Noida and
 Ghaziabad, effective retroactively from April 1.


•The wage hike was approved for workers engaged in 74 scheduled
 employments in the two districts, applying to both contract and permanent
 workers, with payments based on the new rates to be made between May 7 and
 May 10.


•Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath took a dual approach of crackdowns and concessions,
 while also calling the violence a "conspiracy" to derail the state's development.

Noida Workers’ Protest
•Following the protests, UP approved a three-tier minimum wage
 system effective April 1, notified on April 18 after Governor’s assent.


•Gautam Buddh Nagar (Noida) and Ghaziabad are in the top bracket:
 ₹13,690 (unskilled), ₹15,059 (semi-skilled), ₹16,868 (skilled) per
 month.

Noida Workers’ Protest
•The Gautam Buddh Nagar administration moved to cancel licenses of 203
 contractors and blacklist firms across 24 factories for labour law violations.


•The labour department ordered contractors to pay ₹1.16 crore in worker dues and
 warned of court prosecution for payment norm violations.


•Authorities clarified that only EPF and ESI deductions are permitted, and
 workers are entitled to double overtime, bonuses, and gratuity.

Noida Workers’ Protest

•To address concerns about temporary fixes, the state has announced plans to form
 a Wage Board tasked with developing a long-term salary structure that reflects regional
 cost-of-living differences.
•The Labour Department has begun audits of industrial units to identify contractors
 who skim wages or fail to deposit EPF/ESI contributions, while pushing for direct bank
 transfers to ensure workers receive their full pay.
•The district administration has established sector-wise grievance committees where
 factory owners, worker representatives, and labour officials meet weekly to resolve local
 disputes.

Noida Workers’ Protest
•MSME entrepreneurs in Noida and Greater Noida have flagged rising costs and
 policy imbalance following the wage hike, warning that abrupt decisions are pushing
 industries toward ‘near-zero viability’.
•Industry representatives noted that while wages have been raised by ₹3,000, the
 addition of bonuses and ESI pushes the effective increase to over ₹6,000, creating
 a heavy burden on businesses already under pressure due to the Iran war.
•They have sought a two-month pause on inspections and a special relief
 package, warning that without government support, units may be forced to shut
 down or relocate.

Noida Workers’ Protest
•What sets these protests apart is the absence of major trade union
 leadership, which is unusual for labour movements in India.
•The protests have also taken on a pan-India character, with similar
 demonstrations breaking out in Manesar (Haryana), Barauni (Bihar), and Panipat
 (Haryana), highlighting a broader worker discontent across industrial hubs.
•The protests point to deeper strains in India’s labour market, with
 government data showing that around nine in 10 Indian workers earn less than
 ₹25,000 a month, underscoring how low earnings remain for much of the
 workforce.

Noida Workers’ Protest
•The protests have highlighted the delayed implementation of the Code on
 Wages, 2019, and the need for a legally binding national floor wage to ensure
 uniformity across states.
•The incident has also exposed the weak enforcement of labour laws, particularly
 in the informal sector, which employs more than 310 million people in India.
•The formation of a Wage Board in Uttar Pradesh and the push for direct bank
 transfers to workers could serve as a model for other states to address similar
 grievances.

India’s New Deportation
         Policy

India’s New Deportation Policy

•The Union Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has formulated a new
 deportation policy to expedite identification and deportation of illegal migrants,
 particularly from Bangladesh and Myanmar.
•The policy, formalized through the Deportation Manual 2026 issued on April
 2, 2026, provides a standard operating procedure for detecting, detaining, and
 deporting illegal migrants.
•The move follows the Pahalgam terror attack (April 2025) and the
 regime change in Bangladesh (August 2024), which heightened focus on
 domestic security.

India’s New Deportation
                    Policy
What is Deportation? –
•Deportation is a formal legal process where a foreigner staying illegally is
 identified, detained, and removed from the country in accordance with law.
•Under the Citizenship Act, 1955, an “illegal migrant” is a foreigner who
 entered India without valid documents or stayed beyond the permitted period.
•Since citizenship falls under the Union List, the MHA oversees deportation and
 delegates responsibilities to state authorities.

India’s New Deportation
                      Policy
•Illegal migration began with large-scale movements during Partition (1947) from
 East Pakistan, followed by a major influx during the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation
 War.
•Concerns over demographic changes led to the Assam Movement (1979–1985),
 demanding detection and deportation of illegal immigrants from Assam.
•The movement culminated in the Assam Accord (August 1985),
 fixing March 24, 1971 as the cut-off date for identifying illegal migrants.

India’s New Deportation
                      Policy
•Since the 1990s, porous borders with Bangladesh and Myanmar, along with
 economic and political instability, have sustained migration.
•The National Register of Citizens (NRC) for Assam, published in 2019,
 excluded nearly 19 lakh applicants as foreigners, but its implementation remains
 uncertain.
•The issue is now linked with security, identity politics, and resource pressures,
 prompting stricter measures like border fencing and deportation drives.

India’s New Deportation
                      Policy
•Unregulated migration may place pressure on public resources such as food
 distribution, healthcare, and housing.
•Large-scale undocumented influx alters local demographics, creating socio-
 political tensions with indigenous and tribal communities in border states.
•Possession of voter IDs by non-citizens raises serious questions about the
 sanctity of electoral rolls in high-migrant constituencies.

India’s New Deportation
                      Policy
National Register of Citizens –
•The NRC is an official register of Indian citizens in Assam, prepared under
 Supreme Court supervision with March 24, 1971 as the cut-off date, as per
 the Assam Accord (1985).
•The final NRC, published in 2019, included 3.11 crore persons out of 3.30
 crore applicants, excluding over 19 lakh people.
•The NRC has not been formally notified for nationwide implementation and
 remains limited to Assam.

India’s New Deportation
                      Policy
•Those excluded from the NRC can appeal before Foreigners’ Tribunals
 (FTs) , quasi-judicial bodies empowered under the Foreigners Act, 1946, to
 declare a person a foreigner.
•Over 1.65 lakh persons have already been declared foreigners by FTs, and
 more than 85,000 cases are still pending.
•FTs are unique to Assam and play a crucial role in the deportation process, as
 the new policy's holding centre guidelines apply to those declared foreigners by
 these tribunals.

India’s New Deportation
                   Policy
India’s Land Borders –
•India shares a total land border of approx. 15,106.7 km with seven
 neighbours: Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and
 Afghanistan.
•The longest border is with Bangladesh (4,096.7 km) and the shortest
 with Afghanistan (106 km).
•17 states and UTs have international borders; the BSF, ITBP and SSB guard
 different frontiers.

India’s New Deportation
                     Policy
•India’s coastline has been re-assessed from 7,516.6 km to 11,098.81 km by
 the National Hydrographic Office using modern GIS data.
•Gujarat has the longest revised coastline (2,340.62 km), followed by
 Tamil Nadu (1,068.69 km) and Andhra Pradesh (1,053.07 km).
•India’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) is approx. 2 million sq. km, extending
 200 nautical miles from the coast.

India’s New Deportation
                      Policy
Highlights of Policy–
•States must set up a special task force in each district under police
 supervision to detect, identify, and deport illegal migrants from Bangladesh and
 Myanmar.
•These task forces must submit a monthly status report to the Centre on
 foreigners who are missing or overstaying their visas.
•Task forces operate under the District Magistrate, who is designated as the
 competent authority to verify citizenship claims.

India’s New Deportation
                      Policy
•An upper limit of 90 days is fixed to verify the antecedents of suspected
 Bangladeshi or Myanmar nationals.
•States must verify credentials of suspected illegal immigrants within 30 days;
 failure results in automatic deportation proceedings.
•If no credential report is received within 30 days, the Foreigners Registration
 Office can proceed with deportation.

India’s New Deportation
                        Policy
•States must set up holding centers with a 10-feet-high barbed wire boundary
 and strict access control for undocumented migrants awaiting deportation.
•Centers cannot be run from jails; private buildings can be hired if government
 land is unavailable. Basic amenities must be ensured.
•Crucially, members of the same family must not be separated and must be
 housed together.

India’s New Deportation
                       Policy
•A dedicated Foreigners Identification Portal (FIP) has been launched to
 capture biometric and demographic details of intercepted illegal foreigners.
•The District Police Module (DPM) has been launched in over 700 districts to
 track illegal migrants efficiently.
•Data will be shared with UIDAI, the Election Commission, and the MEA to
 prevent future issuance of documents to deported individuals.

India’s New Deportation
                         Policy
•Documents obtained illegally by migrants, such as Aadhaar, PAN cards, and
 driving licenses, must be uploaded for cancellation.
•Deported individuals will be blacklisted by the Bureau of Immigration to
 prevent future entry into India.
•The Bureau of Immigration will publish a list of deportees on a public portal for
 transparency.

India’s New Deportation
                       Policy
•Migrants intercepted at land or maritime borders will be immediately sent
 back after biometric capture, without court process.
•Inadvertent crossers, if found innocent after interrogation, may be handed over
 to border forces of respective countries.
•Illegal immigrants detected near the zero line or within 12 hours of entry will be
 pushed back immediately.

India’s New Deportation
                          Policy
•The guidelines for holding centers also apply to those declared foreigners
 by Foreigners’ Tribunals (FTs) , which are unique to Assam.
•Assam has over 82,000 cases pending in FTs, prompting a separate SOP
 under the Immigrants (Expulsion from Assam) Act, 1950.
•Under the new SOP, Deputy Commissioners can issue expulsion orders within 10
 days, bypassing lengthy tribunal processes.

India’s New Deportation
                       Policy
•The Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025 replaces four older laws: the
 1920 Passport Act, 1939 Registration Act, 1946 Foreigners Act, and 2000
 Carriers’ Liability Act.
•The Act mandates compulsory reporting of foreign nationals by hotels,
 educational institutions, and healthcare facilities.
•It provides statutory backing to the Bureau of Immigration to identify,
 detain, and deport illegal migrants.

India’s New Deportation
                      Policy
•Individuals using or supplying forged passports or visas may face 2 to 7 years
 of imprisonment and fines of ₹1 lakh to ₹10 lakh.
•Anyone entering India illegally without valid documents faces up to 5 years in
 prison and a fine of up to ₹5 lakh.
•The Act also introduces a statutory national floor wage under the Code on
 Wages (relating to labour law).

India’s New Deportation
                       Policy
•Under Article 258(1) , the Centre has delegated the power to identify and
 deport illegal foreign nationals to state governments.
•The Foreigners (Tribunals) Order, 1964 empowers District Magistrates to
 set up tribunals to determine if a person is a foreigner.
•India is not a signatory to the UN Refugee Convention (1951) or its 1967
 Protocol, and states cannot grant "refugee" status.

India’s New Deportation
                        Policy
•Millions of Indians, especially those born before the mid-1980s, lack standard
 birth certificates, leading to harassment of genuine citizens.
•Cases have been reported where Indian citizens with Aadhaar and voter ID
 were deported to Bangladesh without proper verification.
•Police in several states insist on passports or birth certificates for proof of
 citizenship, which many poor families do not have.

India’s New Deportation
                              Policy
•Deportation requires the “parent country” (Bangladesh or Myanmar) to officially accept
 the individuals as their citizens.
•If the origin country denies nationality, individuals risk becoming stateless, languishing
 indefinitely in holding centres.
•Rohingya deportees face acute risk of statelessness, as Myanmar does not recognize
 them as citizens.

India’s New Deportation
                        Policy

•Holding centers have historically faced allegations of poor living conditions;
 prolonged detention of children and women raises ethical concerns.
•The principle of non-refoulement (not returning individuals to persecution) is
 part of international customary law, yet India's pushback policy violates it.
•Despite India’s election to the UN Human Rights Council (2026–28), such
 measures risk undermining its international image.

India’s New Deportation
                       Policy
•District police and local administrations lack capacity and training for nationality
 verification within the strict 90-day timeline.
•This risks delays, increases case pendency, opens avenues for corruption, and
 disproportionately affects vulnerable groups.
•The Supreme Court has intervened in cases of wrongful deportation, directing
 repatriation of Indian citizens.

India’s New Deportation
                    Policy
•The government must ensure transparent verification using multiple data
 points to prevent harassment of genuine Indian citizens.
•Aadhaar, voter ID, land records, and school certificates should be accepted as
 valid proof of citizenship for marginalised communities.
•Technology like biometric databases should improve accuracy while
 guaranteeing procedural safeguards under Article 21.

India’s New Deportation
                       Policy
•India must engage diplomatically to establish a streamlined SOP for smooth
 and timely acceptance of deported nationals.
•Bilateral repatriation agreements should be negotiated to prevent statelessness
 and ensure structured deportation.
•A domestic refugee law should be enacted to distinguish genuine asylum
 seekers from illegal economic migrants.

India’s New Deportation
                     Policy
•Preventing illegal infiltration at the source requires implementing the
 Comprehensive Integrated Border Management System (CIBMS) and
 smart fencing.
•India shares a free-border agreement with Nepal and a Free Movement
 Regime (FMR) with Myanmar (10 km on either side), requiring careful
 review.
•Strengthening documentation with robust verification mechanisms for Aadhaar
 and voter ID, including police checks, is essential.

India’s New Deportation
                             Policy
•The new deportation policy strengthens India’s legal and institutional framework to identify
 and remove illegal migrants, addressing security concerns and resource strains in
 border states.
•However, its successful implementation depends on transparent verification processes,
 respect for human rights, and effective diplomatic engagement with neighboring countries
 to prevent statelessness.
•Balancing national security imperatives with humanitarian obligations and protection of
 genuine Indian citizens remains the central challenge for policymakers.

Passage:
In 2026, industrial clusters in Noida and Greater Noida witnessed significant worker
protests across multiple sectors, including electronics, garments, and automobile
manufacturing. The protests were triggered by a combination of delayed wages,
layoffs, and concerns over contract labour practices. Demonstrations were
concentrated in key industrial zones, drawing attention to labour conditions in
rapidly expanding manufacturing hubs near the National Capital Region.
Reports indicated that several units faced disruptions as workers gathered to
demand timely payment and improved working conditions. Authorities intervened to
restore order and initiated dialogue between employers and worker representatives.
The protests also highlighted the growing dependence on contractual employment
in industrial areas and the challenges of balancing industrial growth with labour
welfare.
